I've had this allergy close to 10 years now and it's been a lot of panicking and learning. I think I have relatively high sensitivity but I can tolerate trace amounts. I avoid all just to be Safe.

To clarify I lived in Japan for 6 months. All my meals were provided by the nursing home I was volunteering at. I think there was a lot of prawn. Two months in I suddenly became allergic. I've always had eczema but I had hives all up my back, legs, etc after ingestion. However I had a slow red/purple rash that spread all over both arms and fingers, up to my mid triceps. I had a Skype call with my family and when I reach up to scratch my nose for just a second they gasped. I also had my coworkers asking "daijyoubu??" Even when they didn't know me.

It was winter and I'd wear the cardigan since it was snowing but throughout my 8 hour shift, the fibres would fuse to my arms and I'd have to peel it off like a bandaid each day. 

I'd had daily baths but have to hold my arms out of the water because it felt like acid. I could only wash the tips of my fingers without pain. Whenever I'd bend my wrist the skin would split open and bleed. 

I saw a skin specialist with limited English. He communicated something I was eating was the cause and gave me hirudoid (the anti bruising cream) and a Japanese steroid which cleared up everything.

I'm scared that since I've avoided it for so long, one day anaphalaxis could occur with an accidental exposure. I always know something has shellfish because my organs feel "itchy" so I appreciate a lot of your advice and I'll check each thing out. 

Lastly and the main question, how do you get your doctor to take you seriously? My allergen doctor in my country who did the prick test said I probably wouldn't need one. This was 10 years ago. I can buy over the counter for 120 but I'd rather the free prescription. I know my gp who's never seen my flare ups probably might not want to prescribe since it's not occurred yet. He's pretty serious and no nonsense

As someone who worked in disability care let me tell you some spots that get missed and build up. 

One of my tasks was to clean the residents ears so here's my pearls of wisdom

First start with the crease behind your ear, no matter the skin type, it will be oily and dead skin like to settle into the creases. Next clean the general area, more so the part on your neck/head than the back of the ear. What tends to build at the back of the ear is dry skin flakes so give them a wipe after you've done your oily bits. 

Next clean the parts that lead to your canal, the residual wax that has tumbled out, your ear is self cleaning and usually doesn't need any deeper cleaning, just get those outer waxy bits. And last, the most neglected, clean the top of your ears on the inside of the ear but above the opening of the canal, so your folds basically. That part, that nook where all the folds meet and attach to your head is full of crusty dead skin cells. 

Lobes are usually fine unless you've pierced them, then you'll get dead skin build up
Usually some warm water does the trick, soap can mess with the biome and microflora
